claims.text: Introducing SRO precipitates into SiC will decrease its lattice thermal conductivity.
Pristine cubic SiC is a relatively high-thermal-conductivity semiconductor.
SRO precipitates can be incorporated into SiC through controlled alloying or post-synthesis heat treatment.
Phonon conduction can be the dominant heat-transfer mode in SiC under the proposed temperature conditions.
An appropriate precipitate size and spatial distribution will effectively scatter phonons.
Introducing SRO precipitates creates interfaces in the SiC matrix.
Introducing SRO precipitates creates lattice distortions in the SiC matrix.
SRO-precipitate interfaces and associated lattice distortions act as phonon-scattering centers.
Enhanced scattering at SRO-precipitate interfaces reduces the phonon mean free path.
A reduced phonon mean free path lowers lattice thermal conductivity.
SiC containing engineered SRO precipitates will have significantly lower lattice thermal conductivity than pristine SiC.
The predicted conductivity reduction is caused by decreased phonon scattering times.
The effectiveness of phonon scattering depends critically on precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction.
Excessive precipitate formation or an inappropriate precipitate size may cause other property degradation or insufficient phonon scattering.
SiC has phonon-dominated heat transport and is sensitive to microstructural alterations.
Similar SRO-induced reductions in lattice thermal conductivity might occur in other semiconductors or insulators.
